purpose: Plan, evaluate, sequence, and validate the concrete decision and build work-units for shipping a Python-first cross-platform app to iPhone, macOS, Windows, Android, and Linux, including stack selection, packaging, signing, store compliance, distribution, and update delivery.
assumptions: Python-first lens: prefer a Python stack, treating native code as a bounded fallback where a platform requires it.
Primary targets are iPhone/Mac/Windows apps; Android and Linux are modeled as in-scope cross-platform targets.
No measured build, performance, or store-rejection dataset is supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors.
Nodes are concrete decision/build work-units, each sized for one heavy reasoning session.
exclusions: Backend/server engineering and API design beyond app-side capability integration.
Detailed native Swift/Kotlin production development beyond the context a Python developer needs.
Game-engine-specific pipelines (e.g., Unity) and pure-web SPA development.
Marketing, ASO copywriting, and monetization strategy.

competency_questions.question: Which platforms must the app ship to and through which distribution channel for each?
For a given platform, is a Python-first stack viable, and where is native code or a non-Python path required?
Which Python mobile and desktop UI frameworks fit the chosen platforms and requirements?
How is platform-independent core logic separated from framework-specific UI?
Which device/OS capabilities does the app need and how are they reached from Python?
How is the app packaged into an installable artifact for each target, including native dependencies?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answerable from MOBILE_PACKAGING_BUILD, DESKTOP_PACKAGING_BUILD, DEPENDENCY_NATIVE_MODULES, DESKTOP_INSTALLER_DISTRO

competency_questions.question: What signing identities, provisioning, and secret handling are required to install and distribute?
Does the app meet store review and privacy-compliance policies for each closed platform?
How are installers built and how do shipped apps safely receive updates?
How is a release coordinated, staged, and monitored across all target platforms?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answerable from RELEASE_ORCHESTRATION, DISTRIBUTION_CHANNEL_DECISION, STORE_COMPLIANCE, AUTO_UPDATE

competency_questions.question: How is the app verified across devices, form factors, and accessibility requirements?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answerable from TESTING_DEVICE_MATRIX, ACCESSIBILITY_COMPLIANCE, UI_LAYER_DESIGN, PLATFORM_CAPABILITY_INTEGRATION

competency_questions.question: Will the app meet startup, memory, battery, and bundle-size budgets given Python runtime overhead?

glossary.definition: BeeWare's packaging tool that wraps a Python app into a native installer per platform
a tool that packages Kivy/Python apps into Android (.apk/.aab) and iOS artifacts via python-for-android/kivy-ios
a freezer that bundles a Python desktop app and interpreter into a standalone executable or folder
an Apple artifact binding an app ID, signing certificate, entitlements, and devices for install/distribution
Apple's automated scan that lets a signed macOS app pass Gatekeeper
a hybrid approach embedding web UI in a native shell with a JS-to-native bridge
a Python library exposing common device features (camera, GPS, notifications) cross-platform
a declared capability/permission an app requests, tied to its signing and store review
PyInstaller modes: a single self-extracting binary versus a directory bundle
releasing to a fraction of users before full distribution to catch defects early
the separation between platform-independent logic and framework-specific UI
a module imported dynamically that a freezer must be told about explicitly

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from Python app-engineering practice and official framework docs (Kivy, BeeWare/Briefcase, Qt for Python), buildozer/PyInstaller usage, Apple/Google distribution guidelines, and Beazley & Jones 'Python Cookbook'; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Decide which platforms (iPhone, iPad, macOS, Windows, Android, Linux) the app must ship to and the priority order among them.
contradictors: dev who codes before scoping platforms

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when distribution goals or target-user device mix changes

pros.claim: every later stack and packaging decision is constrained by the platform set, so fixing it first prevents wholesale rework
pros.example: choosing iPhone-first rules out pure-Python-on-iOS-without-packaging paths early

cons.claim: committing to too many platforms inflates complexity and dilutes a Python-first approach
cons.example: adding Android+Windows+macOS+iOS at once quadruples the signing and store surface

failure_modes: silent assumption of desktop-only or mobile-only
acceptance_tests: platform set is explicit and ranked
each platform has a minimum OS version

nodes.definition: Decide how the app reaches users per platform: App Store, TestFlight, direct download, enterprise/MDM, package managers, or sideload.
contradictors: dev who assumes direct download works on iOS

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when an audience type or store-policy change alters viable channels

pros.claim: channel choice dictates signing, review, and update mechanics downstream
pros.example: choosing the App Store forces notarization, review, and store metadata work

cons.claim: locking a channel before knowing review constraints can force a late stack change
cons.example: picking direct-download for iOS is infeasible and wastes the whole packaging plan

failure_modes: assuming a closed-platform channel that does not exist
acceptance_tests: each platform has exactly one primary channel

nodes.definition: Assess whether a Python-first stack can actually ship to each chosen platform and where native code or a non-Python path is required.
contradictors: dev who assumes CPython runs unmodified on iOS

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a platform's Python runtime support or store policy changes

pros.claim: early viability verdicts prevent committing a whole project to a Python path a platform cannot ship
pros.example: confirming iOS needs a packaged CPython via Briefcase/Kivy before writing app code

cons.claim: viability can degrade silently as OS versions and store rules change
cons.example: an iOS update tightening JIT/dylib rules can invalidate a prior verdict

failure_modes: overestimating Python parity with native APIs
missing a hard capability gap until late
acceptance_tests: each platform has a viability verdict
every gap names a native fallback

nodes.definition: Select the Python mobile framework (Kivy, BeeWare/Toga, or a hybrid/WebView path) for the mobile targets.

included: Kivy vs BeeWare vs hybrid tradeoff

contradictors: dev who picks a framework by GitHub stars alone

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a framework's mobile support, maintenance status, or store compatibility changes

pros.claim: framework choice fixes the widget model, look-and-feel ceiling, and packaging path
pros.example: Toga renders native widgets while Kivy draws its own; the choice sets UX expectations

cons.claim: Python mobile frameworks lag native and can constrain UI fidelity and platform integration
cons.example: Kivy's custom rendering can feel non-native and complicate accessibility

failure_modes: choosing a framework incompatible with the packaging path
acceptance_tests: framework decision cites the viability verdict

nodes.definition: Select the desktop GUI toolkit (PyQt/PySide, Tkinter, Toga, or wxPython) for the desktop targets.

included: PySide/PyQt vs Tkinter vs Toga tradeoff

contradictors: dev who ignores Qt licensing

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a toolkit's licensing, platform support, or maintenance status changes

pros.claim: toolkit choice fixes widget richness, native-look, and packaging compatibility on desktop
pros.example: PySide6 gives native widgets and a rich set; Tkinter ships with CPython but looks dated

cons.claim: PyQt's GPL/commercial licensing or Tkinter's limited widgets can block product goals
cons.example: shipping closed-source on PyQt without a commercial license is a licensing violation

failure_modes: choosing a toolkit that bloats the installer
acceptance_tests: toolkit decision records the licensing basis

nodes.definition: Acquire the native iOS/Swift, Android, and WebView-bridge knowledge a Python developer needs to reason about capabilities, limits, and integration points.
contradictors: Python dev who refuses to learn any native concepts

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a native platform changes APIs, permissions, or lifecycle behavior

pros.claim: native literacy lets a Python dev predict which features need a bridge or native module
pros.example: knowing iOS background-execution limits explains why a Python loop cannot run freely

cons.claim: shallow native knowledge can produce wrong assumptions about what Python can reach
cons.example: assuming Android intents are reachable from pure Python without a bridge

failure_modes: missing a permission or entitlement need
acceptance_tests: each capability gap maps to a native mechanism

nodes.definition: Package the Python mobile app into an installable artifact (.ipa/.apk/.aab) using buildozer, Briefcase, or python-for-android toolchains.
contradictors: dev who builds only on their own laptop

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when toolchain, NDK/SDK, or dependency versions change

pros.claim: a reproducible packaging config is the prerequisite for signing, testing, and store upload
pros.example: a pinned buildozer.spec lets CI rebuild the same .apk on demand

cons.claim: native-dependency compilation on mobile toolchains is fragile and version-sensitive
cons.example: a C-extension wheel without an Android build recipe breaks the whole package step

acceptance_tests: all dependencies bundle or are flagged

nodes.definition: Package the Python desktop app into a standalone distributable using PyInstaller, Briefcase, or similar freezers.
contradictors: dev who ships a bare .py and a requirements file

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when GUI toolkit, Python, or freezer versions change

pros.claim: a clean frozen bundle is what installers, signing, and updates all wrap
pros.example: PyInstaller onedir bundles the interpreter so end users need no Python

cons.claim: freezers miss dynamic imports and data files, producing bundles that break at runtime
cons.example: a plugin loaded by string name is dropped unless declared as a hidden import

failure_modes: data files omitted from the bundle
acceptance_tests: frozen bundle launches on a clean machine
hidden imports and data files are declared

nodes.definition: Generate, manage, and apply code-signing identities, certificates, and provisioning profiles required to install and distribute on each platform.
contradictors: dev who emails a private key around

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when certificates expire, accounts change, or entitlement requirements shift

pros.claim: correct signing is mandatory for install and store acceptance and gates all distribution
pros.example: an Apple Distribution cert plus matching profile is required before any TestFlight upload

cons.claim: key and profile mishandling is high-risk and hard to reverse, and leaked keys force revocation
cons.example: a lost signing key or revoked cert can break every installed copy's update path

failure_modes: leaked or lost private signing key
acceptance_tests: credentials are stored in a secret manager

nodes.definition: Ensure the app meets App Store / Play Store review policies: privacy disclosures, content rules, runtime restrictions, and metadata requirements.
contradictors: dev who submits without reading review guidelines

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when store policies or privacy regulations change

pros.claim: meeting review policy is the gate between a built app and an installed one on closed platforms
pros.example: completing privacy nutrition labels is mandatory for App Store acceptance

cons.claim: opaque, changing review rules cause unpredictable rejections that block release
cons.example: a runtime that downloads executable code can be rejected under iOS code-execution rules

acceptance_tests: privacy disclosures match actual data use

nodes.definition: Build platform-native installers and packages (DMG/PKG, MSI/EXE, deb/rpm) and the channels to distribute them.
contradictors: dev who ships a raw zip of the frozen folder

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when OS installer formats, notarization rules, or branding change

pros.claim: native installers give users a trusted, double-clickable install and enable signing/notarization
pros.example: a notarized DMG installs on macOS without Gatekeeper warnings

cons.claim: each OS has distinct installer tooling, multiplying build and maintenance effort
cons.example: an unnotarized macOS app is blocked by Gatekeeper despite valid code signing

failure_modes: installer not notarized and blocked by Gatekeeper
acceptance_tests: installer runs on a clean target OS
each OS has its native format

nodes.definition: Design and implement the update delivery mechanism so installed desktop/mobile apps can move users to new signed versions safely.
contradictors: dev who ships with no update path

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when signing keys rotate or update-server/version scheme changes

pros.claim: a verified update channel lets shipped apps receive security fixes without manual reinstall
pros.example: a signed Sparkle/Squirrel feed verifies each update before applying it

cons.claim: a broken or unsigned update path can brick installs or push malicious code
cons.example: an update that fails signature checks but installs anyway is a supply-chain hole

acceptance_tests: store-managed updates use the store, not a side channel

nodes.definition: Design the app's screen structure, navigation, and responsive layout within the chosen framework's widget model.
contradictors: dev who hardcodes one screen size

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when navigation model or target form factors change

pros.claim: a framework-aligned UI design avoids fighting the toolkit's widget model later
pros.example: designing Kivy layouts in kv with size hints scales across phone form factors

cons.claim: designing UI before fixing the framework forces rework when widgets do not exist
cons.example: a custom control assumed available in Tkinter may need a third-party widget

failure_modes: layout breaks on unanticipated form factor
acceptance_tests: layouts adapt to target form factors
widgets exist in the chosen toolkit

nodes.definition: Integrate device/OS capabilities (camera, notifications, filesystem, sensors) via Python APIs, plyer, or native bridges.
contradictors: dev who assumes all device APIs are pure-Python

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when OS permission models or capability APIs change

pros.claim: mapping each capability to a concrete access path reveals where native bridges are unavoidable
pros.example: plyer exposes the camera cross-platform but falls back to a bridge for unsupported sensors

cons.claim: capability access through Python wrappers can lag native APIs and miss newer features
cons.example: a new iOS permission may have no plyer wrapper and require a custom bridge

failure_modes: capability unreachable from Python without a bridge
acceptance_tests: each required capability has a working access path

nodes.definition: Decide and validate how third-party and native (C-extension) dependencies are obtained, cross-compiled, or replaced for each target.
contradictors: dev who pip installs without checking platform wheels

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a dependency adds native code or drops a platform wheel

pros.claim: validating dependency feasibility early prevents a packaging-stage dead-end on native modules
pros.example: confirming a numpy build recipe exists for Android before depending on it

cons.claim: native modules may have no cross-compile recipe, forcing substitution or scope cuts
cons.example: a C-extension with no Android recipe can block the entire mobile build

failure_modes: native dependency has no platform build recipe
acceptance_tests: every dependency has a per-target feasibility verdict
native modules have recipes or substitutes

nodes.definition: Set and validate startup time, memory, battery, and bundle-size budgets given Python runtime overhead on each platform.
contradictors: dev who ignores cold-start time on mobile

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when bundle size, runtime, or platform resource limits change

pros.claim: explicit budgets catch Python's startup and memory overhead before users do
pros.example: measuring a 3s Kivy cold start lets you decide whether a splash or native shell is needed

cons.claim: Python runtime overhead can exceed mobile budgets and force architectural change
cons.example: a large interpreter+deps bundle can blow a phone app's size and cold-start budget

acceptance_tests: startup and memory are within budget

nodes.definition: Manage build-time and runtime secrets (API keys, signing keys, tokens) so they are never embedded insecurely in a distributed binary.
contradictors: dev who hardcodes an API key in a .py file

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a secret is exposed, rotated, or a new credential is added

pros.claim: keeping secrets out of the shipped bundle prevents extraction from a distributed binary
pros.example: storing a token in iOS Keychain instead of the .py source blocks trivial extraction

cons.claim: a hardcoded secret in a frozen Python app is easily extracted and hard to rotate post-ship
cons.example: strings in a PyInstaller bundle reveal any embedded API key

failure_modes: key cannot be rotated without a new release
acceptance_tests: no secret is embedded in shipped code
runtime secrets use platform secure storage

nodes.definition: Define and run the test matrix across real and virtual devices, OS versions, and form factors to catch platform-specific breakage.

excluded: unit test authoring of business logic

contradictors: dev who tests only on one simulator

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a new device/OS target is added or a platform-specific defect appears

pros.claim: a real-device matrix catches packaging and capability defects that simulators hide
pros.example: an .apk that works in the emulator may crash on a real device with a different ABI

cons.claim: device fragmentation makes full coverage costly and some breakage only appears on hardware
cons.example: a sensor bug may reproduce only on specific Android OEM builds

failure_modes: platform-specific crash missed by limited matrix
acceptance_tests: each target OS/form factor is exercised

nodes.definition: Coordinate the end-to-end release: versioning, changelog, staged rollout, store submission, and post-release monitoring across platforms.
contradictors: dev who ships all platforms at once with no rollout

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a release fails, a rollback is needed, or a platform's release process changes

pros.claim: orchestrated, staged releases limit blast radius and tie all platforms to one coherent version
pros.example: a 5%-then-100% Play Store rollout catches a crash before it reaches everyone

cons.claim: releasing all platforms simultaneously with no staging makes any defect maximally costly
cons.example: a bad build pushed to 100% of users requires an emergency store re-review to fix

failure_modes: defect reaches all users with no staging
acceptance_tests: monitoring is live before full rollout

nodes.definition: Separate platform-independent core logic from platform/UI code so the same Python core ships across mobile and desktop targets.
contradictors: dev who interleaves UI calls into core logic

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a new platform is added or the abstraction leaks platform specifics

pros.claim: a clean core/UI boundary lets one tested Python core serve every platform's thin UI
pros.example: keeping file I/O behind an interface lets mobile and desktop share the same core

cons.claim: a leaky abstraction couples core logic to one platform and blocks reuse
cons.example: calling a desktop-only API from core breaks the mobile build

failure_modes: abstraction leaks platform specifics into core
acceptance_tests: core has no direct platform/UI imports

nodes.definition: Ensure the app meets accessibility requirements (screen readers, contrast, focus order) within the chosen framework's a11y support.
contradictors: dev who treats accessibility as optional polish

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when UI changes or accessibility standards/regulations change

pros.claim: early a11y design avoids costly retrofits and meets store and legal accessibility expectations
pros.example: exposing labels to VoiceOver/TalkBack during layout is cheaper than retrofitting

cons.claim: some Python UI frameworks have weak native a11y, capping achievable compliance
cons.example: Kivy's custom rendering can lack native screen-reader hooks

acceptance_tests: screen reader can traverse all controls
contrast and focus order meet targets

edges.why_related: channels are chosen per platform, so the platform set must exist first
edges.benefit_of_coupling: fixes channel scope before account setup
edges.risk_of_conflict: choosing channels before platforms forces redo

edges.why_related: viability is assessed per chosen platform
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scopes the Python question to real targets
edges.risk_of_conflict: assessing viability for the wrong platform set wastes effort
edges.example: fix platforms, then test Python viability

edges.why_related: desktop GUI choice only matters once desktop targets are confirmed
edges.benefit_of_coupling: prevents toolkit work for unshipped desktop
edges.risk_of_conflict: choosing a toolkit for a dropped platform wastes work
edges.example: confirm desktop targets, then pick toolkit

edges.why_related: framework choice depends on which Python paths are viable per platform
edges.risk_of_conflict: picking a framework a platform cannot run forces a redo

edges.why_related: dependency feasibility is bounded by the platform's Python runtime
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ties dependency strategy to real runtimes
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring runtime limits yields unbuildable deps
edges.example: fix viability, then plan native deps

edges.why_related: viability gaps determine how much native knowledge is needed
edges.benefit_of_coupling: focuses native study on real gaps
edges.risk_of_conflict: without it, native study is unfocused

edges.why_related: packaging toolchain is determined by the chosen mobile framework
edges.risk_of_conflict: packaging for the wrong framework fails

edges.why_related: freezer config depends on the desktop toolkit's runtime needs
edges.risk_of_conflict: freezing for the wrong toolkit misses libs

edges.why_related: you sign the produced mobile artifact
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures a buildable artifact exists to sign
edges.risk_of_conflict: signing nothing or an unbuilt artifact fails

edges.why_related: you sign the frozen desktop bundle
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures a bundle exists to sign
edges.risk_of_conflict: signing before freezing is impossible

edges.why_related: the channel dictates which signing identities and entitlements are required
edges.risk_of_conflict: wrong identity for the channel blocks distribution
edges.example: derive signing needs from the channel

edges.why_related: store submission requires validly signed artifacts
edges.risk_of_conflict: submitting unsigned artifacts is rejected

edges.why_related: installers wrap signed bundles and may need notarization
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures signed input to the installer
edges.risk_of_conflict: unsigned installers fail notarization

edges.why_related: native knowledge of runtime restrictions predicts review-policy compliance
edges.risk_of_conflict: missing native constraints causes surprise rejections

edges.why_related: installers package the frozen bundle
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures a bundle exists to wrap
edges.risk_of_conflict: building installers before freezing is impossible

edges.why_related: auto-update delivers new installers/bundles, so installers must exist
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures an artifact to update toward
edges.risk_of_conflict: updating with no installer format is undefined

edges.why_related: updates must be signed/verified with the same trust chain
edges.risk_of_conflict: unsigned updates are a supply-chain risk

edges.why_related: UI is built in the chosen framework's widget model
edges.risk_of_conflict: designing UI before the framework forces rework

edges.why_related: desktop UI is built in the chosen toolkit
edges.benefit_of_coupling: aligns desktop UI to the toolkit
edges.risk_of_conflict: UI before toolkit choice forces rework

edges.why_related: integrating device capabilities needs native bridge knowledge
edges.benefit_of_coupling: grounds integration in real platform APIs
edges.risk_of_conflict: integrating without native knowledge produces wrong assumptions

edges.why_related: capability access uses the framework's bridge/plugin mechanism
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ties capability work to the framework
edges.risk_of_conflict: integrating outside the framework model breaks builds

edges.why_related: Python runtime overhead drives the resource budget
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring runtime overhead yields infeasible budgets
edges.example: use runtime facts to set budgets

edges.why_related: the packaged bundle's size and startup feed the budget
edges.risk_of_conflict: budgeting without the real bundle is guesswork

edges.why_related: the build can only bundle dependencies proven feasible
edges.risk_of_conflict: packaging an infeasible native dep fails

edges.why_related: desktop freezing must include feasible dependencies
edges.risk_of_conflict: freezing an unresolved native dep breaks at runtime

edges.why_related: both manage sensitive keys and must use secure storage
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them can leak signing keys via app secrets
edges.example: keep signing keys and app secrets in separate secured stores

edges.why_related: accessibility is audited against the designed screens
edges.risk_of_conflict: auditing a11y before UI exists is premature

edges.why_related: UI screens are exercised across the device matrix
edges.risk_of_conflict: testing UI before it exists is impossible
edges.example: design UI, then test on devices

edges.why_related: device tests run the packaged artifact
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ensures a real artifact to test
edges.risk_of_conflict: testing without a build has nothing to run

edges.why_related: release submission requires a compliant app
edges.risk_of_conflict: releasing a non-compliant app is rejected

edges.why_related: release decisions depend on test-matrix results
edges.risk_of_conflict: releasing untested builds is high-risk

edges.why_related: orchestrated releases drive users through the update channel
edges.risk_of_conflict: releasing without an update path strands users

edges.why_related: a clean core/UI boundary makes the framework a thin, swappable layer
edges.risk_of_conflict: interleaving core and UI couples logic to a framework
edges.example: fix the boundary, then bind a framework

edges.why_related: the core/UI boundary keeps the desktop toolkit swappable
edges.risk_of_conflict: coupling core to a toolkit blocks reuse
edges.example: fix the boundary, then bind a toolkit

edges.why_related: a budget overrun can trigger revisiting the framework or even the Python path
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring overruns ships an unusable app
edges.example: if budget is unmet after mitigation, revisit framework; stop after one re-selection
edges.resolution_rule: budget overrun feeds back to framework

edges.why_related: a compliance rejection over runtime/code-execution rules can invalidate the Python path
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring it leaves a permanently rejectable app
edges.example: if rejected on runtime grounds, re-open viability; stop after a viable path or platform drop

edges.why_related: secret-handling rules forbid embedding secrets in the frozen bundle
edges.benefit_of_coupling: bounds what the build may include
edges.risk_of_conflict: embedding a secret in the bundle leaks it
edges.example: never freeze secrets into the bundle; inject at runtime from secure storage

conflict_axes.trigger: staying pure-Python conflicts with reaching native-only capabilities and store acceptance
resolution_order: confirm the capability cannot be reached from Python
prefer a thin native bridge over abandoning Python
abandon Python only when a platform forbids the runtime
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Python-first dominates until a hard capability or policy gap forces a bridge or native path
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a platform policy forbids the Python runtime entirely
conflict_axes.example: missing camera/notification access in pure Python

conflict_axes.trigger: maximizing shared cross-platform code conflicts with delivering a fully native look and a11y per platform
resolution_order: share the core logic always
share UI only where native fidelity is acceptable
branch UI where native look or a11y demands it
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: shared core dominates; UI may diverge per platform when native fidelity or accessibility requires it
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a shared widget cannot meet a platform's a11y bar
conflict_axes.example: a custom-drawn control feels non-native on iOS

conflict_axes.trigger: pressure to ship fast conflicts with completing review, privacy, and signing requirements
resolution_order: never bypass signing or privacy disclosure to ship faster
stage rollout to absorb review delays
accept slower release over rejection risk
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: compliance and signing dominate ship speed for closed platforms
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a deadline tempts skipping privacy disclosures
conflict_axes.example: submitting without privacy labels to hit a date

conflict_axes.trigger: single-file/simple bundles conflict with fast startup and small resource footprint
resolution_order: measure startup and size against the budget
prefer onedir when onefile blows the startup budget
mitigate before changing the framework
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the resource budget dominates packaging convenience when budgets are breached
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if startup exceeds the agreed threshold after mitigation
conflict_axes.example: PyInstaller onefile extracting to temp slows cold start

conflict_axes.trigger: embedding secrets for convenience conflicts with keeping them out of an extractable binary
resolution_order: never embed secrets in the shipped bundle
inject at runtime from platform secure storage
rotate any exposed secret immediately
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: secret security dominates packaging convenience without exception
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a secret would be compiled into the bundle
conflict_axes.example: an API key left as a literal in a frozen module

conflict_axes.trigger: using rich native dependencies conflicts with portable, buildable packaging on every target
resolution_order: prefer dependencies with platform build recipes
substitute pure-Python where feasible
cut a dependency before cutting a platform
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: portability dominates dependency richness when a native module blocks a required platform
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a native dependency has no recipe for a required target
conflict_axes.example: numpy/scipy lacking an Android build recipe

conflict_axes.trigger: a custom self-update mechanism conflicts with store policies that require store-managed updates
resolution_order: use store-managed updates on closed platforms
use signed self-update only on direct-download channels
never side-load code on a store platform
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: store policy dominates custom self-update on closed platforms; self-update is for direct channels only
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if self-update would download executable code on a store build
conflict_axes.example: a Sparkle-style updater inside an App Store build

conflict_axes.trigger: broad real-device coverage conflicts with testing cost and release timelines
resolution_order: cover the highest-traffic device/OS tiers first
use staged rollout to catch the long tail
expand the matrix on observed platform defects
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: risk-weighted coverage dominates: high-traffic tiers must pass before release; the tail is caught by staged rollout
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if an untested high-traffic tier remains before full rollout
conflict_axes.example: skipping the most common Android OEM build

edge_cases.trigger: a platform forbids the packaged Python runtime or dynamic code execution
edge_cases.example: an iOS rule blocks downloading/executing code, rejecting a Python-bundled app
edge_cases.detection_method: check store runtime and code-execution policies during viability, before building
resolution: choose a compliant packaging or native path

edge_cases.trigger: a native C-extension dependency has no cross-compile recipe for a target
edge_cases.example: a C-extension wheel with no python-for-android recipe breaks the .apk build
edge_cases.detection_method: resolve every dependency's per-target feasibility before packaging

edge_cases.trigger: a secret is embedded in the frozen/packaged binary
edge_cases.failure_mode: API key extractable from the distributed app
edge_cases.example: strings on a PyInstaller bundle reveal a hardcoded token
edge_cases.detection_method: scan the bundle for known secret patterns before signing
resolution: inject at runtime from secure storage

edge_cases.trigger: a certificate or provisioning profile expires before or during release
edge_cases.failure_mode: installs and updates fail to verify
edge_cases.example: an expired Apple Distribution cert blocks TestFlight upload mid-release
edge_cases.detection_method: monitor certificate/profile expiry dates against the release calendar

edge_cases.trigger: an update is applied without verifying its signature
edge_cases.example: an updater installs a tampered package because signature checks were skipped
edge_cases.detection_method: assert signature verification is enforced before any update is applied

edge_cases.trigger: a dynamically imported module or data file is dropped by the freezer
edge_cases.failure_mode: app crashes at runtime on a clean machine
edge_cases.example: a plugin loaded by string name is missing from the PyInstaller bundle
edge_cases.detection_method: launch the frozen bundle on a clean machine and exercise dynamic paths in CI
resolution: add data files to the spec

edge_cases.trigger: a macOS app is signed but not notarized
edge_cases.example: users see a 'cannot be opened' warning on an unnotarized DMG
edge_cases.detection_method: verify notarization status of the macOS package before distribution

edge_cases.trigger: a build depends on unpinned local toolchain state
edge_cases.failure_mode: CI cannot reproduce the shipped artifact
edge_cases.example: an .apk built only on one laptop with an unpinned NDK cannot be rebuilt
edge_cases.detection_method: rebuild from a clean CI environment and diff the artifacts

edge_cases.trigger: Python runtime overhead pushes startup or size past the budget
edge_cases.failure_mode: app feels slow or exceeds store size limits
edge_cases.example: a 3s+ Kivy cold start exceeds the agreed startup budget on mid-range phones
edge_cases.detection_method: profile startup, memory, and bundle size against the budget table on real devices
resolution: escalate to framework re-selection if unresolved

edge_cases.trigger: platform-specific calls leak into the shared core
edge_cases.failure_mode: one platform's build breaks the shared core
edge_cases.example: a desktop-only file API called from core breaks the mobile build
edge_cases.detection_method: build the core in isolation for each target and forbid platform imports in core
resolution: move platform calls behind the abstraction

edge_cases.trigger: UI is built before the framework/viability is settled
edge_cases.failure_mode: UI work is discarded when the framework changes
edge_cases.example: screens designed in one toolkit are scrapped after a framework switch
edge_cases.detection_method: check priority_order: no downstream node finalized before its prerequisites

workflow.objective: fix the platform set, priorities, and distribution channels
acceptance_tests: platform set is explicit and ranked
each platform has a primary channel
workflow.do_first_because: every downstream stack and packaging decision is constrained by platforms and channels

workflow.objective: decide where Python is viable and where native code or substitution is needed
acceptance_tests: each platform has a viability verdict
every native dep has a feasibility verdict
workflow.do_first_because: committing to a Python path a platform cannot ship is the most expensive late failure

workflow.objective: select frameworks and fix the core/UI boundary
workflow.do_first_because: framework and boundary choices set the widget model and reuse ceiling for all later work

workflow.objective: build the UI and integrate device capabilities
acceptance_tests: layouts adapt to target form factors
each capability has a working access path
workflow.do_first_because: UI and capability work proceed once the framework model is fixed

workflow.objective: produce reproducible packaged/frozen artifacts within the resource budget
acceptance_tests: startup and size are within budget
workflow.do_first_because: a reproducible, in-budget artifact is the prerequisite for signing and testing

workflow.objective: sign artifacts and secure all build/runtime secrets
acceptance_tests: no secret is embedded in shipped code
workflow.do_first_because: signing and secret discipline gate all distribution and cannot be retrofitted safely

workflow.objective: verify the app across devices, form factors, and accessibility
acceptance_tests: each target OS/form factor is exercised
screen reader can traverse all controls
exit_criteria: test matrix and a11y audit pass
workflow.do_first_because: release decisions must rest on real-device and accessibility evidence

workflow.objective: achieve store compliance, build installers, and wire the update path
entry_criteria: signed artifacts and QA results available
exit_criteria: compliance passed, installers and updates ready
workflow.do_first_because: compliance, installers, and a verified update path must exist before any release

workflow.objective: coordinate a staged, monitored release across platforms
entry_criteria: compliance, installers, updates, and QA complete
acceptance_tests: monitoring is live before full rollout
workflow.do_first_because: staged, monitored release limits blast radius and ties all platforms to one version

priority_rationale.notes: root scope all later decisions inherit
viability gates the entire stack path
prevents packaging dead-ends on native modules
fixes mobile widget model and packaging
fixes desktop toolkit and freezing path
builds screens within the chosen framework

dominance_rules.trigger: release pressure tempts skipping signing or store/privacy compliance
dominance_rules.rule: compliance and signing dominate ship speed on closed platforms
dominance_rules.required_action: complete signing and review requirements before submitting
dominance_rules.example: skip privacy disclosures to hit a launch date

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value node lacks an unmet prerequisite
dominance_rules.rule: true dependency precedence dominates value-first ordering
dominance_rules.required_action: schedule prerequisites before dependents regardless of value
dominance_rules.example: building UI before the framework is chosen

dominance_rules.trigger: a preferred Python path is not viable on a required platform
dominance_rules.required_action: use a bridge or native path where the platform forbids the Python path
dominance_rules.example: forcing pure Python where the store bans the runtime

dominance_rules.trigger: embedding a secret would be convenient
dominance_rules.rule: secret security dominates packaging convenience without exception
dominance_rules.required_action: inject secrets at runtime from secure storage; never embed them
dominance_rules.example: hardcoding an API key into a frozen module

dominance_rules.trigger: an unsigned update would restore availability faster
dominance_rules.required_action: block any update that fails signature verification
dominance_rules.example: applying an unverified hotfix to restore service

dominance_rules.trigger: a node is ready to lock but lacks passing tests
dominance_rules.required_action: do not soft/hard-lock a node before its acceptance tests pass
dominance_rules.example: locking a build before device testing

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-risk or irreversible decision is reached
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation for high-risk/irreversible steps
dominance_rules.required_action: require human approval for signing, compliance, updates, and release
dominance_rules.example: auto-approving a 100% rollout with no human sign-off

dominance_rules.trigger: a numeric estimate looks precise but is heuristic
dominance_rules.rule: correct evidence labels dominate apparent numeric precision
dominance_rules.required_action: label all estimates heuristic; never claim observed without data
dominance_rules.example: labeling a guessed cold-start time as observed

dominance_rules.trigger: adding more nodes would breach schema or budget
dominance_rules.rule: schema stability and JSON validity dominate added density
dominance_rules.required_action: keep counts within density bounds and the schema valid
dominance_rules.example: padding near-duplicate framework nodes to inflate the count

dominance_rules.trigger: a rich native dependency blocks a required platform
dominance_rules.rule: portability dominates dependency richness for required platforms
dominance_rules.required_action: substitute or drop the dependency before dropping a required platform
dominance_rules.example: keeping a native lib that has no Android recipe

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix the platform set before choosing any framework or packaging path
anti_rework_rules.rationale: stack choices are constrained by platforms; choosing first forces wholesale redo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: framework chosen for a platform later dropped
anti_rework_rules.example: selecting Toga before knowing desktop is in scope

anti_rework_rules.rule: confirm Python viability before selecting a mobile framework
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a framework on a non-viable platform is wasted work
anti_rework_rules.example: picking Kivy before checking iOS runtime support

anti_rework_rules.rationale: packaging an infeasible native dependency dead-ends the build
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: build fails on an unbuildable native module
anti_rework_rules.example: packaging numpy on Android without a recipe

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix the core/UI boundary before building UI
anti_rework_rules.rationale: UI built into core logic blocks cross-platform reuse
anti_rework_rules.example: calling platform APIs directly from core

anti_rework_rules.rule: choose the framework before designing screens
anti_rework_rules.rationale: UI built for the wrong widget model is discarded on a framework change
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: screens scrapped after a framework switch
anti_rework_rules.example: designing in Tkinter then moving to PySide

anti_rework_rules.rule: produce a reproducible artifact before signing
anti_rework_rules.rationale: signing requires a stable artifact; signing a moving target wastes effort
anti_rework_rules.example: signing before pinning the build config

anti_rework_rules.rule: sign and notarize before building installers or submitting to stores
anti_rework_rules.rationale: unsigned artifacts fail notarization and store review
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: installer or submission rejected for signing
anti_rework_rules.example: submitting an unsigned build to review

anti_rework_rules.rule: define secret handling before packaging anything for distribution
anti_rework_rules.rationale: secrets frozen into a bundle are extractable and force a re-release to rotate
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: secret found embedded in a shipped binary
anti_rework_rules.example: an API key compiled into the app

anti_rework_rules.rule: complete the device matrix and a11y audit before releasing
blocked_until: test matrix and a11y audit pass
anti_rework_rules.rationale: releasing untested builds maximizes the cost of any defect
anti_rework_rules.example: shipping after testing only one simulator

anti_rework_rules.rule: require update signature verification before shipping the update path
anti_rework_rules.rationale: an unsigned update path is a supply-chain hole that is costly to retrofit after ship
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: an unverified update applied in the field
anti_rework_rules.example: shipping an updater that skips signature checks

iteration_protocol.trigger: validator or review reports a failure
acceptance_tests: every failure mapped to a subsystem

iteration_protocol.detection: rank defects by risk and downstream rework cost
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue empty or only sub-threshold defects remain

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect touches a locked or high-coupling node
iteration_protocol.detection: trace dependents and edges from the defect node
acceptance_tests: all dependents of the change identified
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: impact set stable across a pass

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is selected for repair
iteration_protocol.detection: route it via repair_routing to the owning subsystem
re-run the validator and formula recomputation

iteration_protocol.trigger: a node's evidence or risk estimate changed materially
a high-risk or irreversible defect cannot be auto-repaired
acceptance_tests: human approval recorded for irreversible steps

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new KB version is produced
iteration_protocol.detection: compare against the prior version before release
action: check no regression in pass rate

checks.repair_action: modeled python-vs-native and store tensions as conflict_axes and feedback/constraint edges, not dependencies
all derived fields recomputed by formula script to 2 decimals

test_cases.input_summary: ship a Python app to iPhone via the App Store
ship a PySide app to Windows with auto-update
distribute a notarized macOS app outside the store
app needs a capability with no pure-Python path
app depends on a C-extension on mobile
app must call an API with a secret key

version_increment_rules: increment on any hard-locked release change
increment when formulas or metric weights change
lock_downgrade_rules: downgrade dependents when an upstream node changes
downgrade when an evidence label is revised
